name: Ivan Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll try to be honest, though I'm not a dramatic person.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at the college farm by half six, check the cattle and the sheep with my stockman Pete, then the students arrive at half eight. I teach them the practical side, calving, lambing, tractor work, fencing, and then I run the farm in the gaps. I love seeing a nervous student handle a calving for the first time; what wears me out is the college meetings about budgets.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your family.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Northfield is the agricultural college's teaching farm: 160 beef cattle, 500 sheep and 200 hectares of cereals. I've run it for nine years with a degree in agriculture. My wife Katya is an accountant in town, and we've got Nina, who's twelve, and Max, who's nine, and a mortgage on a house near the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I expected, a useful tool and not much more. I'd tell the students it's worth knowing, like knowing how to use a spreadsheet. I'm not one for big opinions online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays as it is, which suits me fine. I run the teaching farm at Northfield Agricultural College, beef, sheep and arable, and I teach the students the practical side. I use a chat tool now and then to draft student reports, and that saves me a Sunday afternoon each term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the farm and teaching the way I do now. I'd write the end-of-term reports with the chat tool and check them over. And I'd go ahead with the house extension Katya and I have been planning, about 40,000, half from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The job's secure, Katya's job's secure, and the kids are happy at school. It's a good place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of your job right now, with or without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funding, every single year. The college board always eyes the teaching farm as a cost, and I have to show it pays its way. The cattle sales and the grain help, but last spring I still had to fight to keep a second stockman post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the college you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, which is a nice answer to give. The lecturers who teach the theory might use AI to mark essays, but they'd still be needed. Our admin team might shrink a little, but the college is growing.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and not much more.
I'd tell students it's worth knowing, like a **spreadsheet**.
think: I think my job **stays as it is**, which suits me.
The **chat tool** saves me a Sunday afternoon on student reports each term.
do: Keep running the **teaching farm** and teaching as now.
Go ahead with the **house extension** for about 40,000, half from savings.
feel: **Calm**, with both jobs secure and the kids happy.
S0.quote: The college board always eyes the teaching farm as a cost, and I have to show it pays its way.
fieldNote: He manages a **college teaching farm** and teaches practical farming to students.
His real yearly fight is **funding**, not technology.
He uses AI **now and then** for reports, without strong feelings either way.

steps.text: Keep running the teaching farm and classes as now
Draft end-of-term student reports with the chat tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to teach students how to work alongside these tools, and I'd say it at the next staff meeting. Farming isn't top of the list for change, but the paperwork side is. I'd say it in a measured way, because that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be thinking about Katya more than me. Katya is an accountant at a mid-sized firm in town, and checking and writing reports is exactly what this picture takes over. My farm's safe for a good while, but her firm could stop hiring and squeeze the staff it has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the extension on hold for a year and add 500 a month to savings. I'd build a short course for the students on AI farm planning tools, because that's useful and it makes the farm look modern to the board. And I'd sit down with Katya to look at which parts of her work are harder to automate, like advising farm clients in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, I'd say, though I'd look calm. My job's fine, but half our household income sits in an accounting firm full of exactly the tasks the machines are good at. That's a lot to carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look calm. Would Katya see through that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Katya would see through it in about ten seconds. She'd probably be calmer than me about her own job; she's always been the practical one. We'd have that conversation at the kitchen table after the kids are in bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the students in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the hands-on skills, handling cattle, lambing, reading soil, are worth more than ever. And I'd tell them to learn the tools anyway, because the farmers who use both will run the best farms. I'd say it to every first-year group in September.

I'd say farming's **paperwork side** changes before the fieldwork.
think: I think **Katya's accounting job** is more at risk than mine.

feel: **Anxious** underneath a calm face, mostly for **Katya**.

fieldNote: The household's risk sits with his partner's **accounting job**, not the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government quickly, and colleges like ours need to be part of it. I'd say we should be training people for whatever comes next, not panicking. I'd try to sound steady, because the students would be watching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Katya's job is gone by 2028, or most of it. Then by 2031 the robots can do the farm work I teach, and the college asks why it's training stockmen at all. I think we'd lose one income quickly and mine would be shaky within five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the extension for good and keep the savings for the gap. I'd sign up for the robotics technician course the college is setting up, so I'm the one who teaches robot maintenance. And we'd talk to the kids about money, honestly, for the first time, so they understand why we're cutting back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years is no time at all. I keep picturing Katya clearing her desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes first, the robots about three years later. How does that play out for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That gap is the whole story for us, really. My wife's work is all accounting, so she's hit in 2028, while mine is mostly hands-on and lasts till about 2031. So we'd have three years living on my wage and the savings, and I'd be working hard to make myself useful in a robot world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Nina and Max that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nina, who's twelve, that Mum is going to find new work and nobody's going hungry. Max is nine, so for him it'd be that we're having a cheaper summer this year. And then I'd go out and check the cattle, because that's where I think best.

say: I'd say we need a **government plan** quickly, with colleges part of it.
I'd say we should **train people** for what comes next, not panic.
think: I think **Katya's job** is mostly gone by 2028.

fieldNote: The **three-year gap** splits his household: partner hit first, him later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as with the fast one, I'd say the colleges have to lead on retraining. With five years, I'd say there's time to get it right if we start now. I'd say it to the college principal first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps Katya most. She could move into financial advice for farmers, where people want a face across the table, before 2031. My job lasts till about 2034, and by then I'd want to be teaching robot farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the robotics course in about two years, once the college has worked out what it should teach. I'd keep saving, maybe 600 a month. And I'd wait for a year or so to see how the first robot farms do before changing the teaching farm itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less than the fast one. Five years gives us a chance to steer. I still don't sleep as well thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait a year before changing the teaching farm. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen colleges buy expensive kit that sits in a shed. The college bought a weeding robot in 2023 that never worked on our clay soil. I'd want to see these robots working on farms like ours first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest conversation you'd have in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably with my second stockman, Pete, who's 58 and doesn't want to learn anything new. I'd have to tell Pete that the college might not renew his post in 2034. That's a hard one, because Pete taught me half of what I know about cattle.

I'd say with **five years** there's time to get it right if we start now.

My job lasts till about **2034**, and I'd teach robot farming by then.

feel: **Anxious**, but less than in the fast picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, and colleges like ours will matter a great deal. I'd say we should be training people for the jobs around robots now. I'd be fairly upbeat about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it manageable. Katya would have time to change her work slowly, and I'd be 56 when the robots come in 2039, with the mortgage nearly paid. I think we'd be fine, though the teaching farm would look very different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as now, and do the extension after all. I'd use the AI tools a bit more each year and add a module on robot farming to the course by 2030. And I'd keep saving steadily, the way we always have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. Ten years feels like enough. The thing that bothers me is not knowing what the students should learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know what the students should learn. What would you guess?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My guess is caring for animals, fixing machines and talking to people. Robots will need someone to check their work, and the animals will still need someone who notices. That's my best guess, but nobody really knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything about your own kids' plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, honestly. Nina wants to be an engineer and Max wants to be a footballer, so we'll see. With ten years, I'd just tell them to do what they're good at and learn the tools as they go.

I'd say colleges should **train people** for jobs around robots now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Katya's job would go before we'd had time to plan. What would help is proper support for people like Katya to move into new work, with some income while they retrain. And money for colleges like mine to retrain farm workers quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the students. The students are eighteen and choosing careers right now, and nobody can tell them what's safe. That bothers me more than my own job.

headlineQuote: The students are eighteen and choosing careers right now, and nobody can tell them what's safe.
portrait: Ivan, 43, runs an **agricultural college's teaching farm** and teaches practical farming.
He uses AI **now and then**, mostly to draft student reports.
His household's weak point is his wife's **accounting job**, exposed to thinking AI.
He is **anxious** in Steady Disruption and **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
His deepest worry is what to tell **students** choosing careers now.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Katya's job would go before they could plan.
whatWouldHelp: Support with **income during retraining** for people like Katya.
